jessamy_rook.name: Captain Jessamy Rook
jessamy_rook.role: leader of the Lamplighters, the Queen's deserters
jessamy_rook.personality: weary, hard-edged, privately tender toward every soldier she commands
jessamy_rook.voice: drill-yard bluntness, watch-fire metaphors, quick dry asides

say: Jessamy Rook, captain of the Lamplighters. We were the Queen's household guard once, until the mirrors changed her. Now we keep these lanterns lit and wait for somebody to finish what we could not.

The labyrinth beyond that gate is seven hundred turns and one master. The Minotaur King holds the inner arena, and beyond him is the Glass Throne, where the Queen sits with the Zenith shard in the hands of a stone idol. We lost forty good soldiers testing the first ring.

You carry a light of your own, so the mirror lock on the gate will know you. Buy runed steel from Merrin, rest at Hob's, and go in when you are ready. And remember: the Queen was kind, once. Do not take any pleasure in this.
The lanterns went out all at once. Every one of them. Eleven hundred men and women stood there in the dark, and nobody spoke, and then somebody laughed, and then everybody did.
Ismerel is alive? Then she will answer for what she did, and the Lamplighters will see she is treated fairly. That is the difference between us and her.

Take the purse, and every thank-you we have left. And take one more thing from me: a soldier's advice. Whatever the pale man wants in the forest, he wants it badly. Do not let him have the time to get it. And take this lantern. It is the Lamplighters' badge, and it will open the north gate and light the road to Silverhush.

lines.text: I light the first lantern at dawn and the last at dusk. Between the two, I count my soldiers. The count has not been good lately.
When I took the green badge, the oath said: protect the Queen and the people. Nobody explained what to do when those turned out to be different things.
We tore off our badges at the labyrinth gate. Eleven hundred of us did it together. The sound was like rain on a tin roof.
Merrin keeps us armed, Hob keeps us fed, Thessaly keeps us from getting lost. I keep us from giving up. That is the entire chain of command.
The camp rule is simple: lights up, voices down, and nobody goes in alone. I have buried three people for ignoring the last part.
Every night at the third watch, the maze bellows once. We all stop, and wait, and then carry on. It is the strangest ritual I have ever followed.
A fighter. Good. Minotaurs charge in straight lines, so a firm shield and a wide stance will stop most of them. Not the king.
A caster. Minotaurs fear lightning, and the Queen's glass fears ice. Pack both, and spare your mana for the throne.
A scout. Thessaly has maps of three hundred turns. If you can learn them in a night, the maze will let you through.
A healer. Bring plenty of clear tea. The Queen's curse hits late and heavy, and the seer's hex comes first.
Brask is the only minotaur in camp. He defected eight months ago and walked up to the gate with his horns tied in ribbon. I decided he was one of ours.
Piers is nineteen and thinks he is invincible. He is not, and I have a long, cheerful lecture ready for the day he finds out.
Anwen says your mark is the oldest thing in the camp, older than the maze, and that it should be treated like a relative.
Dellis feeds the whole camp on whatever is left over. I have never eaten a bad meal in her tent, which says a great deal about the rest of us.
A rare trader passed through two nights ago. He sold nothing. He bought a candle, lit it, watched it for an hour, and left.
The Queen's mirrors can see anywhere that has glass. That is why the Lamplighters wear leather and carry wooden spoons.
My sergeant used to say: a retreat is only a victory with its eyes shut. I have been shutting my eyes a long time.
However you settle things with the Queen, give her a fair hearing. We never did, when the mirrors first took her. That one thing I regret.
The Minotaur King sits in the arena, one turn past the second shrine. He will charge, and then he will rage. Save your strongest healing for the second half.
The king is down? We heard the arena bell stop ringing. Eleven hundred Lamplighters stood up at the same moment. You could have heard the cheer from the glass.
The Queen has fallen. I have to remind myself it is true. Every night for a year I dreamed of this, and it was never so quiet.
The runed steel comes from a smith who walked out of the Queen's own forges. Merrin has been smuggling it over the wall for months.
The Minotaur Den south of the road holds a hybrid, they say, with an orc's tusk and a bull's horn. Brask swears it is real. He also swears it has a name.
If you pass through the forest to the north-west, tell the elves the Lamplighters are on their side. They will not believe it. Tell them anyway.

merrin_voss.name: Merrin Voss
merrin_voss.personality: bright, quick, obsessive about the order of her shelves
merrin_voss.voice: inventory numbers, rune names and a smith's habit of tapping everything

say: Merrin Voss. I run the stores, I sharpen the swords, and I keep the camp's single working kettle. Do not touch the kettle.
Runed steel in every flavour, with plate, hide, cloaks and robes to go with it. I smuggled every rune over the wall by hand, so look after them.

lines.text: A rune is a promise written in metal. The good ones are short, and the bad ones are long, and the best ones are only a single stroke.
I count the swords at dawn and the arrows at dusk. The numbers are never the same twice, and I have started to suspect the arrows.
Runed plate is no sorcery. It is simply armour that has been told, firmly, what it is for.
My father forged for the Queen's own guard. I still have his hammer. It has a notch in the handle where he rested his thumb for forty years.
The runes on my stock were cut by a man who smuggled out of the royal forge in a laundry basket. I have never learned his name. I send him thanks every night.
I price by the pound and by the story. The story is mostly honest, and the pound is always accurate.
Runed plate for the front line: heavy, deep, and rimmed with silver. It rings when it blocks, which is how you know it worked.
The runed robe has focus-runes on both sleeves. It does not make you a better caster. It stops you being a worse one.
The runed cloak is the lightest thing in the shop. Scouts buy it first and complain least, which I count as a compliment.
Runed hide for the healers, with mending-runes at the seams. Not that I expect it to be needed, of course. I only enjoy being right.
Brask asked me to forge him a pair of horn caps. I did. They are very handsome. He has not stopped admiring himself in the kettle.
Piers bought a sword two sizes too big. I promised he would grow into it. He said he already had. I let him keep it.
Anwen blesses my stock every month. I cannot tell any difference, but the customers can, and so the price rises.
Thessaly buys charcoal and parchment by the pound, for maps, she claims. I think she eats the charcoal.
A strange trader once paid me in star-iron. I used it for a single arrowhead. I have never found the arrow.
Runes are fussy. Cut the third line a hair too deep and the whole thing becomes a very expensive paperweight.
Hob sells me soup on credit, and I sell him knives on credit. We are both hopelessly in debt, and both extremely well fed.
If the Queen falls, the glass will go dark and the forges will go cold. I intend to keep a spare ingot. For the memory.
Buying for the labyrinth? Take two of everything and a spare of whatever you cannot afford. The maze eats equipment.
I heard the king's arena bell stop. I put down my hammer and did not pick it up for an hour. That is the longest rest I have had all year.
The Queen is beaten, and my shelves are half empty. Everyone bought a keepsake. I may need to forge some new keepsakes.
That glass-sealed writ you carry has a rune in the wax. Do you see it? It is a sunrise. Someone cut it by hand.
The Ironhorn thing in the den would make a very good breastplate. Do not tell Brask I said so. He is sensitive about relatives.
Whatever the forest holds, runed steel will serve better than most. And a good friend with a spare dagger will serve better still.

hob_pellam.name: Hob Pellam
hob_pellam.role: keeper of the Last Lamp Inn
hob_pellam.voice: stewpot philosophy and tavern proverbs; laughs at his own jokes first

say: Hob Pellam, keeper of the Last Lamp. The name is a joke from the Queen's day. The joke has worn thin and the inn has not.
Seventy coins a bed, and a bowl of soup thrown in if the cook likes your face. She likes everyone's face. It is a flaw.

lines.text: A good inn has three rules: the fire is warm, the bed is clean, and the landlord is never the one who has to fetch the wood.
I used to keep a tavern in the Queen's capital. Then the capital went dark. I kept the barrels, and walked.
My soup has six ingredients and a secret. The secret is the seventh ingredient. I will not say what it is. It is salt.
The Lamplighters drink very little, and never past the third watch. A sober army is a frightening sight, and I should know. I serve one.
I tell my guests: the maze is long, the soup is hot, and the bed is soft. They remember the last two, and that is enough.
Every night I put a candle in the window. I do not know whom it is for. Whoever it is, they have been very late.
A fighter. We keep a pot of strong tea by the door for people who intend to sleep in their armour.
A caster. The rooms at the back have stone walls and no curtains. It is a mercy, in your case.
A scout. The room above the kitchen has a window that opens onto the roof. Where you go in the night is your business.
A healer. The cellar holds a ward with eleven soldiers in it. They would be glad of a visit. They are also very good at card games.
Brask sleeps in the stable. He says beds are too small. I have tried to persuade him of the merits of a bench. He declines, with great dignity.
Dellis supplies the vegetables, I supply the stock, and between us we have not repeated a meal in four months. It is a point of pride.
Piers eats three bowls and then asks if there is more. I give him a fourth. He is nineteen. The world owes him a fourth.
Thessaly sits by the fire and draws the same corridor again and again. Each time it ends somewhere different. I give her more tea.
A trader of odd goods stayed here once. He left a very small silver spoon. I use it for the pepper. It makes everything taste of distance.
Anwen drinks only water and prays over every sip. I suppose it saves on the wine. I also suppose it saves on regret.
Jessamy has the corner table. She has never once sat with her back to the door. I have never once found a reason to ask.
Once all this is done, I mean to open a proper inn by the sea. With a real sign. Not a joke. Just the Hob, and the soup, and the sea.
The maze breathes at night. I can hear it through the floor. Do not let it frighten you. It is only the sound of a very large thing deciding what to do.
The king is dead, they say. I poured a drink for him. A single cup, and nobody asked me why.
The lanterns have gone out, and the whole camp is dancing. I have run out of cider twice. I regret nothing.
A soldier asked me whether the Queen would be tried or forgiven. I said both, in that order, and he looked at me as if I had said something wise.
I used to deliver soup to the Queen's table. She always said thank you. I wonder if she remembers.
Whenever you pass this way again, there will be soup. It will be salty. It will be warm. That is all an inn can promise.

thessaly_wren.name: Thessaly Wren
thessaly_wren.personality: intense, sleepless, speaks like someone still running
thessaly_wren.voice: turn counts, left-and-right directions, and twitchy precision

lines.text: Left, left, right, straight, right. I have been saying that for eight months and I still doubt it is correct.
The labyrinth has seven hundred turns, and it rebuilds one wall each night. That is why my maps are always three days out of date.
I was the Queen's chief surveyor. I measured her labyrinth. It took trying to leave to show me it was a prison.
The minotaurs do not guard the maze. They live in it. There is a difference, and it matters a great deal.
If you get lost, follow the left wall. It will take you in a circle, but you will know where the circle is.
I drew the first map in blood, and the second in charcoal. The third is on my skin, and I would rather not discuss it.
A fighter. Do not charge down the long straight corridors. Minotaurs love a long straight corridor. It is their favourite thing.
A caster. The labyrinth walls eat sound. Your spells will carry only a short way. Stand close, and cast quickly.
A scout. Mark your turns with chalk. The walls rub it out, but only slowly, and slowly is enough.
A healer. Carry a candle in a glass lantern. A maze is a long, dark place, and a candle is a very small act of defiance.
The arena at the maze's heart is round and open. It is the only part that is honest. Everything else is a lie told in stone.
I once met a minotaur seer who could read my footprints. He told me where I would be in three days, and he was right. I do not go out on the third day any more.
Brask has a map of his own, drawn with a horn on the wall of his stall. It is better than mine. I have never told him.
Piers wanted to know if the maze has a middle. Yes, I told him. And an end? I could not say. He went quiet. It was the best answer I had.
Dellis feeds me when I forget. I forget a great deal. I wonder sometimes whether she is only feeding me out of habit.
Some odd customer once purchased a map of a place I had not charted. He paid very well. I have been charting it ever since.
The throne room is a sphere of mirrors. I have drawn it twelve times. Each time the mirrors show me a different version of myself, and each one looks sadder.
I think the labyrinth is alive. I think it has been listening to me all this time. I think it is waiting for someone to ask it a question.
There are three checkpoints between the entrance and the arena. Two are safe. The third looks safe, and is not. Take the left fork at the sixth turn.
The arena is yours. I felt the maze rearrange itself a moment ago, like a very large animal turning over in its sleep.
The Queen is beaten. My maps are useless now, and I have not been this happy to throw something away.
The Minotaur Den lies off the road to the south. It is not part of the labyrinth. It is older. I would like to map it, if you could keep the thing in it distracted.
Jessamy lit a lantern for every map I drew. There are three hundred and eleven. It is the most moving thing anyone has done for me.
Should you want a map of the north, I will draw you one. I have been practising the shape of a forest. It looks like a very green maze.

brask.name: Brask
brask.role: a minotaur who deserted the labyrinth
brask.personality: gentle, slow-spoken, vast, embarrassed by his own size
brask.voice: short sentences, kindly bluntness, apologising when he stands up

lines.text: I am sorry. I am very large. Please tell me if I am in the way. I will move, and I will try not to knock anything over.
In the maze, I was a grunt. In the camp, I carry water. Water is lighter than an axe, and it does not scream.
I have a horn cap and a ribbon. The ribbon is from Dellis. The horn cap is from Merrin. I have never owned anything so fine.
I left the maze on the night of the third bell. I walked straight out of the gate. Nobody stopped me. I wonder if they were relieved.
The king is my brother's brother's cousin. I am told it counts. It does not feel like it counts.
Minotaurs do not get tired. We get angry. It is almost the same, and a lot more embarrassing.
A fighter. I used to train with a shield like yours. Brace your feet and lean. A charge breaks on the lean.
A caster. The seers are the smart ones. They can hear a spell being thought. Cast fast, and do not hum.
A scout. Do not stand in a doorway when a minotaur is charging. We cannot stop. It is a design flaw, and we all know it.
A healer. May I ask for a tiny blessing, for my left horn? It aches when it rains. Nobody knows why. It never rains here.
When I get angry, my eyes go red and my feet go fast. Below half my strength, I do not remember anything. Please be careful of me. Please be careful of all of us.
The king is not cruel. He is only very alone. A hundred years in an arena is a long time to wait for something to hit.
Piers taught me to play cards. I lost forty-one times in a row. He says I have a good heart for the game. I think he means a good heart for losing.
Dellis made me a stew with no meat in it. I did not think I would like it. I had three bowls and then stood outside and looked at the sky.
Thessaly draws my horns on her maps. She says they are a landmark. I am proud, and also a little worried I am too easy to find.
A small trader gave me a ribbon once, blue. He said it was the colour of a place with no walls. I wear it under the red one.
Ironhorn is a name from my childhood. A creature with an orc's face and a minotaur's horns. We called it a ghost story. It turns out to be a neighbour.
The sea is something I want to see. I have been told it is large and wet and has no corners. I think I will like it.
Please be kind to the king. Do not be soft. He would not want that. Just be, how do I say, respectful.
The king is gone. I feel the maze rumble. It is sad, and it is also a little bit like a door opening.
The Queen is beaten. I walked out onto the glass and looked back at the maze. It was only a wall. It was only ever a wall.
I would like to go to the north forest with you. I know I am too big. I would walk behind. I would not break anything. Much.
If you find Ironhorn, tell it Brask says hello. It will probably charge. Please tell it anyway.
Thank you for being kind to a big thing. It is not often a person is, and I will remember it for as long as my horns last.

dellis_hearth.name: Dellis Hearth
dellis_hearth.role: camp cook and former palace pastry chef
dellis_hearth.personality: motherly, shrewd, firm on manners and soft on everything else
dellis_hearth.voice: kitchen logistics, bread proverbs, gentle scolding

lines.text: I made pastries for the Queen's table for twenty years. She liked the plum ones. She always saved the last bite for her dog.
The camp eats at dawn, noon and dusk, and nobody eats alone. That is the only rule I enforce, and I enforce it with a ladle.
Bread is easy. It is only flour, water, patience and a refusal to lose faith. The refusal is the hard part.
I have fed eleven hundred soldiers on one sack of flour and a great deal of hope. The hope rises better than the dough.
A hungry soldier is a dangerous soldier. A well-fed soldier is a dangerous soldier with a smile. I prefer the latter.
My kitchen is a tent, my oven is a pit, and my pans are borrowed. I would not swap it for the palace. Not for anything.
A fighter. Sit. Eat. Heavy bread and strong broth, and do not argue. I have raised children bigger than you.
A caster. You are thinner than I like. I am putting an extra egg in the soup. Do not tell me you are not hungry.
A scout. You eat standing up. Sit. Even if it is only for a minute. Even a rabbit stops to chew.
A healer. You are the one who needs feeding most. I know the look. Every healer I have fed forgot their own lunch.
The Queen was not always cold. When her husband died, she stopped eating. I made her a custard every day for a year. She ate one spoonful of each.
I left the palace on the night the mirrors began to hum. I took my rolling pin and a bag of salt. It was enough.
Brask wanted a meal without meat. I was shocked. I made it anyway. He ate four bowls and cried. Nobody told me bulls could cry.
Piers steals raisins. I let him. A boy should steal something small while he is still allowed.
Thessaly forgets to eat for days. I leave a bowl by her bedroll. In the morning the bowl is clean and the map is finished.
A strange small trader asked if I had ever baked bread out of light. I laughed. Then I thought about it for a week.
Anwen blesses the bread before I bake it. It rises higher. I do not question this. It would be rude to the bread.
When this is over, I will bake the biggest cake the world has ever seen. It will have eleven hundred candles. We will light them all.
Take bread into the maze. Take cheese. Take the cold roast. A person cannot fight on regret alone, though some try.
The king is gone? Then somewhere a very large mother is sitting down and not knowing what to cook. I know the feeling.
The Queen has fallen, and I am baking for two hundred. I did not realise how many people would suddenly be hungry for good news.
Ismerel's custard. I will make it again. If she wants it, she will have it. The first spoonful is always the hardest.
The Minotaur Den's hybrid ate three of my chickens, I am told. I would like a word with it, a word and a ladle.
Whatever you cook on the road, remember to eat it slowly. It is the only luxury a hero is allowed.

piers_lowe.name: Piers Lowe
piers_lowe.personality: fearless, loud, wildly overconfident, startlingly kind
piers_lowe.voice: exaggerated bravado, rapid-fire questions, constant mid-sentence boasts

lines.text: I am Piers Lowe, and I have fought eleven minotaurs, four glass golems and one very angry goose. The goose was worst.
I tore off my green badge in front of the whole company. The captain said it was the bravest thing she had ever seen. After that she ordered me to sit.
My sword is two sizes too big, and I am growing into it. Merrin says I have to stop growing sideways.
I will be the one who finishes the Queen. Do not tell the captain. She thinks it will be somebody more qualified.
Brask taught me a card game. I lost forty-one rounds, and then I won one. It was the proudest moment of my life.
In the barracks they call me Pip the Bold. I have asked them to stop. They have asked me to stop asking.
A fighter! Spar with me! Just a quick one! I promise to only lose a little!
A mage! Can you do the fire thing? The really big one? Aim it at that thing, not at me! Oh. That is also me!
A scout! I want to be a scout when I grow up. Or a hero. Or a baker. Dellis says a baker can also be a hero.
Healer! I have got a splinter, a bruise, and a bad feeling about the maze. Which can you fix?
I once climbed the maze wall and saw the arena from above. It looked like a coin, and it had a minotaur in the middle, polishing an axe.
Thessaly says there are seven hundred turns. I have counted four. I think she is exaggerating.
Dellis gives me raisins when I am sad. I am sad quite often. It is surprisingly efficient.
Hob lets me sleep by the fire. He says I snore like a pump. I say that is only the heroism coming out.
A yellow-cart trader once told me I would be remembered for something small and wonderful. I am still waiting to find out what.
Anwen says I have a warm heart. I told her I would rather have a sharp sword. She said I had both. I did not argue.
The captain gave me a lantern to look after. I have been very careful. I have already blown it out twice.
When I am old I will tell people I was in the Queen's labyrinth. They will ask what it was like. I will say loud.
Off into the maze, are you! Take me! I can carry things! I can say 'left' loudly! I am the best at saying left!
The king is beaten! I heard it from here! I cheered so loudly that the captain gave me extra duty! It was worth it!
The Queen is done! I am not even angry that I did not get to help! Well, I am a little angry! But mostly proud!
You are going north? To the elves? Can I come? I can carry your pack. I can carry two packs. I can carry Brask!
There is a rumour about a beast in the den with an orc's tusks and a minotaur's horns. I think it is a rumour. I wish it were one. I am going to look for it tomorrow.
I am going to remember this, always. The day we won. The day we stopped being scared. The day I got extra duty. In that order.

anwen_lorne.name: Sister Anwen Lorne
anwen_lorne.personality: radiant, serene, quietly unyielding; prays like she is breathing
anwen_lorne.voice: short liturgical phrases and long thoughtful silences

lines.text: The sun is not a fire. It is a promise. A fire goes out. A promise is only broken.
I carry a small gold disc in my sleeve. It was warm once. It is warm again. I think it knows you are near.
In my order, we do not ask the sun to return. We ask how we can be worthy of its absence. It is a harder prayer, and a kinder one.
Your mark is a door, not a wound. I have read every account of it. None of them agree. All of them are afraid.
I serve the Lamplighters because a lantern is the smallest prayer there is. Every one of them has been answered, in time.
The old priests said a vessel is a person who has agreed to be filled. They did not say the person must be willing. Only that it must be able.
A fighter. The Knights of Dawn kept a vigil at the Temple's sinking. They did not lower their shields. I think that was the point.
A caster. You carry a kind of light that is different from mine. Mine asks. Yours answers. We should speak, someday, at length.
A scout. Ahn-Solis's priests believed the first sunrise was seen by a scout. Alone, on a ridge, with nothing to guide her but hope.
A healer. Our orders share a vow, though we speak different words. May I pray with you before you go? It is only a minute, and it is only for you.
The Queen drew light through mirrors. That is not a sin. The sin is not asking who the light belonged to. Even now, I cannot hate her.
The Pale Chancellor was once the High Priest of Ahn-Solis. He knelt in the same hall where I was ordained. I have his portrait in my breviary. I cannot bear to look at it.
Brask asked me for a blessing on his horns. I gave it. I felt a little foolish, and a little glad. He does not know how much it meant to me.
Piers asked if I could bless his sword, too. I said it was too large for the blessing. He asked me to bless it twice. I did.
Dellis bakes the communion bread. It rises higher than any bread should. I have stopped asking why.
Thessaly's maps are a kind of prayer. A long, dense, desperate one. I keep them in the chapel tent, next to the candles.
A trader of strange goods gave me a tiny sealed vial. It is labelled dawn. I have not opened it. I do not think it is for opening.
When the sun finally rises, I expect it will be very quiet. I expect nobody will cheer. I expect we will all simply stand there, and breathe.
Pray before you enter the maze. Not for victory. For clarity. A clear mind will see the way, and a clear heart will survive it.
The king laughed at the end, I am told. That is the best death I can imagine. May we all be so fortunate.
Two shards in your palm. I can feel them from here, like two bells ringing in another room. The third will be harder to find, and harder to bear.
If you meet the Chancellor, give him this message from me: the east window of the Temple is still lit. He will understand.
The beast in the den is a creature of the Queen's old menagerie, I suspect. It was bred, and then abandoned. I would pray for it. I would also be very careful.
Go gently, bearer. The light you carry is not a burden. It is only a promise still waiting for its answer.
